analysis.one_liner: Strengthens protections against workplace harassment and discrimination and phases out the lower minimum wage for tipped workers.
analysis.headline: The bill, which would also phase out the lower minimum wage for tipped workers, has sat without action in five House committees since its introduction, with no vote scheduled.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would tighten federal workplace civil rights law in several ways. It would require employers to adopt anti-harassment policies and training, make it easier for workers to sue over harassment, let workers recover uncapped damages, extend protections to smaller employers and to interns and contractors, ban forced arbitration and nondisclosure agreements in discrimination cases, and clarify that discrimination based on sexual orientation and gender identity is sex discrimination. It would also phase out the lower "tipped" minimum wage, eventually requiring employers to pay tipped workers the full federal minimum wage plus their tips.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers benefit most: harassment victims get a longer window to sue, an easier legal standard, uncapped damages, and the right to take cases to court instead of private arbitration; LGBTQ workers get explicit statutory protection; tipped workers see their base wage raised each year until it reaches the full federal minimum; and low-income workers get funded legal help. Workers in small businesses, including domestic and gig-adjacent settings, gain coverage because the employer threshold drops from 15 employees to one.

how_it_helps.text: It requires employers with 15 or more employees to adopt and post comprehensive nondiscrimination policies, provide interactive training for employees and supervisors, and face fines of up to $5,000 per violation for willful noncompliance [S2].

It writes a harassment standard into statute: conduct that unreasonably alters the terms, conditions, or privileges of employment is unlawful, judged by the totality of circumstances, so a single severe incident can qualify and courts may no longer dismiss cases for failing a rigid 'severe or pervasive' threshold [S2].

It removes caps on compensatory and punitive damages, extends the time limits for filing claims, clarifies that discrimination based on sexual orientation and gender identity is sex discrimination, and bars the Religious Freedom Restoration Act from being used as a defense in Title VII cases [S2].

It extends nondiscrimination protections to contractors, interns, fellows, volunteers, and trainees; restricts nondisclosure agreements; prohibits mandatory arbitration of discrimination claims; and restores supervisor liability for harassment [S2].

It phases out the separate sub-minimum wage for tipped employees, raising their base cash wage by $1.50 an hour per year until it reaches the full federal minimum wage, and guarantees employees the right to keep their tips [S2].

It funds civil legal assistance for low-income workers facing employment discrimination and creates a system of state advocacy offices, alongside a national survey and research program on the prevalence of workplace harassment [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Employers pay: they must build and run anti-harassment programs, face fines for noncompliance, potentially uncapped damages, expanded liability, and higher wage costs for tipped staff. Restaurant owners bearing the phase-out of the tipped minimum wage bear a distinct share.

drawbacks.text: The bill lowers the threshold for harassment liability, applies a 'motivating factor' standard that lets workers win without proving discrimination was the sole reason for an employment decision, and removes caps on compensatory and punitive damages — changes that would expose employers of all sizes to far more litigation and larger payouts [S2].

Extending civil rights protections to employers with even one employee (down from 15), and to contractors, interns, and volunteers, imposes the full cost of policies, training, and potential liability on very small businesses that have limited ability to absorb it [S2].

It bars the Religious Freedom Restoration Act from being used as a claim or defense in Title VII cases, a provision that drew objections on religious-liberty grounds when similar language was proposed in earlier Congresses [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The main costs are compliance expenses for employers (drafting policies, training, potential fines and larger damages awards) and, for restaurants, the gradual elimination of the sub-minimum tipped wage, which some restaurant owners argue would force price increases or staffing cuts. Weighing this against the bill's aims — restoring workers' ability to sue for harassment, ending forced arbitration and NDAs in discrimination cases, and phasing out a wage structure that leaves tipped workers dependent on customer goodwill — the benefits to workers are substantial and the compliance burdens are the kind employers already face in most states. The most serious design risk is the expansion of damages and liability exposure, which critics argue could raise litigation costs for small firms even when the underlying protections are sound.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and sent to five House committees, none of which took it up, so it never reached a vote in either chamber.

narrative.text: Representative Ayanna Pressley introduced the BE HEARD in the Workplace Act in the House on February 13, 2026, joined by 14 original cosponsors [S2].
The same day, the bill was referred to five committees: Education and Workforce, Judiciary, House Administration, Oversight and Government Reform, and Veterans' Affairs [S4].
The action history shows no further activity after the referrals — no hearings, markups, or floor action — as of the record provided [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, employers who would have faced the new compliance costs, damages exposure, and elimination of the tipped sub-minimum wage are better off, since the bill has not advanced.

sides.party_line_note: Every identified sponsor and cosponsor is a House Democrat; no Republican support appears in the record, but no formal votes have occurred to show a party split.

industries.note: The bill gradually eliminates the lower cash wage for tipped employees, requiring these employers to pay the full minimum wage while workers keep their tips. For a labor-intensive industry this is a significant new wage cost, though workers gain guaranteed pay on top of tips.

industries.industry: Arbitration providers and employers that use mandatory arbitration
industries.note: Employers could no longer force workers into private arbitration for discrimination claims, cutting off a large volume of business for arbitration providers and removing a shield employers have used to keep harassment cases out of court.

All employers with one or more workers face new policy and training requirements, fines, expanded liability for harassment, uncapped damages, and a longer window for workers to sue. Compliance costs fall most visibly on small businesses newly covered by federal nondiscrimination law.

industries.industry: Employment law and civil rights legal services
industries.note: The bill funds legal assistance for low-income workers and state advocacy systems, and its expanded causes of action create more work for plaintiff-side employment lawyers and legal aid organizations.

analysis.trajectory: With no committee action since its February 2026 introduction and a House Rules process controlled by the majority, the bill's realistic path is to remain in committee for the rest of the 119th Congress and expire without a vote, as earlier versions of the same legislation have done.
